title: G-A-L
hookLine: geulah, go'el: redeem, as a relative redeems family land

lines: FOR THOU ART A NEAR KINSMAN.
cards: Midnight, on a threshing floor. The barley harvest is in, and a landowner named Boaz has fallen asleep beside the grain heap. He wakes with a start: someone is lying at his feet.
"Who art thou?" A widow, Ruth, the foreigner who has been gleaning in his field. She doesn't ask for money.
She asks him to spread his cloak over her, and gives her reason in a single phrase: "for thou art a near kinsman." That phrase, near kinsman, is one Hebrew word: go'el. Today's root.

teach.h: THE GO'EL BUYS BACK THE LAND.
teach.b: G-A-L. Gimel, alef, lamed. Go'el, the one who redeems.
Geulah, redemption. Turn it four ways. First, the law behind the word.
In Leviticus, if a man falls into poverty and sells part of his land, "if any of his kin come to redeem it, then shall he redeem that which his brother sold." To redeem is to buy back.
The go'el is the relative who steps in so the family doesn't lose its ground. Second, the gate.
The morning after the threshing floor, Boaz sits at the town gate, because a relative closer than he is has the first right to redeem a field that belonged to Naomi's late husband.
That man is ready to buy the field, until he learns Ruth comes with it. Then he backs away: "I cannot redeem it for myself." Boaz steps in, and the land and the family stay together.
In Egypt, before the plagues, God says to the enslaved people: "I will redeem you with a stretched out arm." God is cast as the near relative who comes to buy the family back. Fourth, the prayer.
In the weekday Amidah, one blessing calls God go'el Yisrael, the redeemer of Israel, and geulah is something Jews still pray toward.
So redemption in this root isn't vague. It looks like a relative walking to the gate and paying what it costs to bring someone home.

how: Jews read the book of Ruth on Shavuot, and the weekday Amidah includes a blessing to God as go'el Yisrael, the redeemer of Israel; geulah, redemption, is a hope that runs through Jewish prayer.

s: in the Torah, a go'el is a near relative who buys back what the family lost
"if any of his kin come to redeem it."
Boaz was the only relative with the right to redeem
a closer kinsman had the first right, and turned it down.
the word for redeem in Exodus is a different word from the one in Ruth
"I will redeem you" uses the same root: God as go'el.

games.q: you're the closer relative at the gate. the field is yours to redeem, but Ruth comes with it. what do you do?
o: redeem it, and take Ruth's family in.
decline: I cannot redeem it for myself.
games.why: he backs away: "I cannot redeem it for myself." Boaz steps in and keeps the land and the family together.

practice: Bring to mind something that slipped from where it should be but could still be bought back: a friendship gone quiet after a sharp word, a promise half kept, your own garden gone to weeds.
Ask what it would cost, a phone call, an apology, an hour, a bit of pride, and settle on the one step you'd take, the way Boaz walked to the gate. If you pray, you can ask for help with it.
